utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar, kindly call the case, please.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Good afternoon, Your Honours. This is case number IT-03-67-T, the Prosecutor versus Vojislav Seselj.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, Madam Registrar. Today we are Tuesday, the 13th of May, 2008. I would like to greet the representatives of the Prosecution, Mr. Seselj, as well as all the people assisting us in the courtroom. We have started half an hour late because of a misunderstanding about the time at which this hearing was due to start. The Registry thought we were starting at a quarter to 3.00. So to avoid this happening again, tomorrow I would like to specify here and now that the hearing will start at quarter past 2.00 p.m. On Thursday, we shall also start at a quarter past 2.00. I would like to let Mr. Seselj know that the internet broadcasts do not work properly at the moment. There seems to be a technical hitch, something which I've been informed about this morning, and I think that it is still the case.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Registrar has just told me that what was not working this morning is now working, the websites are working again properly, which is a good piece of news. Let me now ask the Registry to move for a few moments into private session, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In open session: Mr. Seselj, is your screen working properly, because I was informed about a number of technical problems you had. Can you read the transcript on your screen? Do you have it displayed on your screen in English?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, I'm not following the transcript in English at all on the screen. What I follow is the videotape from the courtroom, because when somebody else is speaking, I get a little help from that.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Your screen is working. Mr. Seselj, do you have a housekeeping matter you would like to address before we start or not?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I have two matters to raise. You've already mentioned that first document that I did not wish to receive because it was in English. The Prosecutor, as for Witness 011, sent me a complete set of documents, a binder with all the documents, and all the listings were in English, and I returned that. Now, it escaped my attention that along with this witness that is supposed to appear today, the list is in English once again. But since there are not a large number of documents, I didn't -- I decided not to make any problems about that. This is happening ever more frequently. Could you put a stop to it, please. And, secondly, for the following week, for next week, we have an expert witness, [indiscernible]. I'm not quite sure whether the Prosecution provided me with the transcripts of all his testimony in other trials, so I demand that you issue instructions to the OTP to prepare, by the break, a list and to prepare a report, and to tell me which documents I have received for what testimony by that expert witness. And the third matter is this: You made it incumbent upon the Prosecution almost a month ago, before the break that we had, that before the beginning, that is to say, this should have taken place last week, that I should be provided with a revised list of the remaining witnesses. We still do not have that, and there is a great deal of misunderstanding, I assure you. Some witnesses were struck off the list. Now, if all the witnesses that were mentioned in this trial were to be added up, it would make over 150 witnesses, but the misunderstanding is great, there's a lot of muddle, and I don't know which witnesses remain. And you instructed the Prosecution to do that. However, they have not done that thus far.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Briefly, I shall address the three points mentioned by Mr. Seselj. As far as the Witness VS-011 is concerned, of course the binders which have been disclosed to Mr. Seselj need to contain,(a), the documents in English and,(b), in B/C/S. From what I understood, Mr. Seselj has sent the binders back because there was nothing in his language. So I must say I'm somewhat surprised about this. But since Witness VS-11 is not coming today, this is not a matter of some urgency. But why is this the case? Those binders which were disclosed to Mr. Seselj, why were they not in English and in B/C/S, according to what Mr. Seselj has told us?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let me just put you right, Mr. President, on one point. The documents were in Serbian and in English, but the introductory part, a review of the documents and a description of the documents was exclusively in English, and that was over several pages.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The table of contents was in English, I believe, is that right, and so have it translated in his language, please. I don't think that should be too much of an issue for you. The second point. As far as the expert witness is concerned, the Trial Chamber has handed down a decision concerning this expert witness, who is due to come and testify. It would be best if the Prosecution could get hold of the statements and witness transcripts of this witness in other case. Is it possible to disclose this in a very short period of time?

utterances.speaker: MS. BIERSAY
utterances.text: I think so, Your Honour.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The third point, the revised list of witnesses. This had not escaped my attention. I shall run through this quickly, because the Trial Chamber started scrutinising all of this. So please note what I am about to say. First of all, the Trial Chamber has set up a list of the remaining witnesses, for the insider witnesses. I shall give you the names of 48, 34, 32, 27, 26, 17, 14, 12, 11 and number 9 are the remaining witnesses. There is one witness whose name I shall not give, who will be a witness of the Court, if his health is good enough. Now, as far as the expert witnesses concerned, Grujic, Whitmeier [phoen], Stankovic, Strinovic, Osman, Tabeau and VS-1112: As far as Vucin and other witnesses are concerned, 018, 031, 030, somebody called Maritic and Matovina, whom we'll hear today, and VS-050 [Realtime transcript read in error 030] -- it's not 030, but 050. There's a mistake in the transcript. 008, 016, 022, 045, 051, a witness called Kovic, a witness called Dozan [phoen], a witness called Panic, a witness called Vojnovic and Vukasinovic is the last one. Now, I must add that from 008 to Vukasinovic, these witnesses are related to Vukovar. All the others -- all the others relate to all the other municipalities. As far as Vuskovici [phoen] is concerned, 35, 53, 54, plus Barisevic [phoen], Kalic, Klasic, Pulic, plus 1141. Now, for Zvornik, we have 37, 38, plus somebody called Buskovic plus 1012, plus Bazanovic [phoen], Fadil, 1063, 1064, 1066, 1087, 1093, plus Seferovic, plus 1105, plus Alic, Asim, and Music, Fadil. For Bijeljina and Berko, there are four witnesses: VS-1028, Dusalic [phoen], Gazi, and 1035. For Bosanski Samac, there is Dagovic, Bisic, Lukac, Tahic, and 1010 and 1058. For Novasin [phoen] Mostar, we have (redacted), 1022, 1024, 1025, 1026, 1051, plus Katic, Dzemal, 1067, 1068, 1069. For the Sarajevo area, we have Kublar [phoen], Masnopita [phoen], Safik [phoen], plus VS-1057, VS-1060, VS-1111, and after the 20th of March we added another witness, who (redacted), and VS-1050. Interpreter's note, all the others relate to the other municipality in the singular. Now, if I totalled all these hours, you would need 135 hours, but according to our calculations, you only have 77 hours left. So we have a real problem here, and I would like to ask the Prosecution to look into this very closely, because you don't have 135 hours left. You have been allotted a certain amount of time, and it is not as much as that, so you need to provide a revised list. You need to give this to the Trial Chamber and to the accused. We need to know where we stand and where we're going. So we have drawn up this list to try to understand clearly where we're going, and for the time being things are not clear to us at all, because if I total the number of hours you have planned to hear these 83 witnesses, whose names or numbers that I have just read out, you would need 135 hours and 30 minutes, and you would go well beyond the time that has been allotted to you. So please look into this and let us know. So I have responded to Mr. Seselj's question, who addressed the issue of the revised list. Mr. Seselj, you would like to have the floor?

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, I wasn't able to follow the whole list of witnesses carefully, but two problems spring to mind straightaway. You mentioned Miodrag Panic for instance as a witness, for instance, but the Prosecutor a while ago tabled a request to have him struck from the witness list. And I informed you a long time ago that Miodrag Panic signed a statement saying that he wanted to be a Defence witness. He is the chief of staff of the 1st Guards Brigade. Then (redacted). Two years ago, the Prosecution gave up on him as a witness and informed me about that in writing, both me and the Trial Chamber, then some time ago it tabled a request that he be put back on the witness list. As far as I remember, I still have not received any Court ruling pursuant to that request and I tabled a motion opposing the Prosecution request. So there are a number of amendments. Some witnesses have died in the meantime. So the Prosecution ought to provide us with a reliable and complete list.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. All the more reason to have this list, so I would like the Prosecution to prepare this promptly, please, that we have a revised list. If we have no more housekeeping matters, we shall bring in the witness that has been scheduled for today. So I shall ask the usher to go and fetch the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good afternoon, sir. Can you give your first name, last name, and date of birth, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] My name is Djuro Matovina. I was born on the 22nd of March, 1949.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, are you currently employed, and if so, what is your job?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Not now. I'm retired.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Sir, have you ever testified before a court of law on those events which unfolded in the former Yugoslavia or is it the first time you come to testify today?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I testified in 2002, in October, in the Milosevic trial.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. I would like you to take the solemn declaration, please.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I solemnly declare that I will speak the truth, the whole truth, and nothing but the truth.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you, sir. You may sit down.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sir, since you have already testified before this Tribunal, you know how this hearing is going to unfold today. To begin with, you will answer the questions that will be put to you by the Prosecutor. I don't know which one of the two people on the Prosecution team will be leading their evidence today, but you will be shown documents, and they would certainly like to hear your comments. After this, Mr. Seselj, who is sitting on your left-hand side, will put questions to you. This is part of what we call the cross-examination. He has the same time as the Prosecution will have to put questions to you. The three Judges that former the Bench can also put questions to you to shed some light on some of your answers. If you have any kind of problem which would warrant an interruption of the hearing, that is fine. Normally speaking, we have a break every hour and a half. Please try and be as concise as you possibly can when you answer a question. If you do not understand the meaning of a question, please do not hesitate to turn to the person who has put to you this question and ask the person to rephrase it. This is what I wish to share with you by way of introduction. I shall now give the floor to the Prosecution, who is going to start its examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Your Honours, I will lead this witness in the examination-in-chief.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, can you tell us what is your nationality and your ethnicity?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I am a citizen of the Republic of Croatia, and my ethnicity is Croatian.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Are you married and do you have children?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I am married, and I have two children.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: I will now come to your professional background. Could you please describe to us what was your profession when you were not resigned?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: My profession is criminologist. I worked in the Ministry of the Interior, and for almost 30 years I worked as a policeman and a crime inspector.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you tell us where you worked in 1989, 1990, and what your position was?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: In 1989 and 1988, I was the acting chief of the police station in Slatina. And in 1990, I was the assistant chief, who was appointed that year, and his name was Stjepan Gojmerac.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you let us know what is the name of the area in which you were working?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The town was called Podravska Slatina. Otherwise, it's the area within the composition of the former Podravska Slatina Municipality, which is today six municipalities, and it is the Virovitica-Podravina County.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What were your tasks and your competences as acting chief of police?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I was in charge of public law and order, crime prevention, traffic safety, administrative affairs that were done at the police station; everything linked to citizens and their affairs within the realm of the police force.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What was the ethnic composition in this area?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: In the area of the former Podravska Slatina Municipality, 36 per cent of the population was Serbs, the majority population was Croatian, and the other ethnicities, 2 or 3 per cent of them were others, mixed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Just a minute, please. Witness, please, could you clarify something for us, please. In 1990, you said you were a criminologist. What was your status? You said you worked for the police. State who you were working for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990, when the chief of the police station became Stjepan Gojmerac, I was assistant chief of the police station; that is to say, the coordinator for the affairs that I set out a moment ago.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, but which state were you in? The state you worked for in 1990, what was the name of the state you worked for.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Socialist Federal Republic of Yugoslavia is what the state was called, and the republic was the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You've told us the percentage of the Serbs, but could you please also let us know what was the percentage of the Croats in that area?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: In the town of Slatina itself, the percentage of Croats was 49 per cent, that of Serbs 47 per cent, and as I have already said, 36 per cent were Serbs, but in the Municipality of Slatina, the Croats accounted for over 60 per cent.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You said on the record -- I read it from the record that the Serbs were 47 per cent and the Croats 49. This is not clear to me. You mentioned in the beginning 36 per cent were Serbs and 46 -- and 49 per cent Croats. Could you clarifies this?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: No problem. Actually, this refers just to the city of Slatina, which was the cultural, political and administrative seat of the former Municipality of Slatina. So the city, which had -- the town which had 10.000 inhabitants had this concentration and national mix. The first figures referred to the Slatina -- to the town, and the others to the entire municipality, which is a broader concept. And the police station in Slatina was in charge of this entire area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, I would like to come back to a question asked to you by my colleague. You answered the question, but I can see from the transcript that there's a mistake. The question was the following: At the time, what state were you working for in 1990? What state were you working for?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was the Republic of Croatia, which was still part of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You've studied criminology. You were chief police inspector. So you have some legal knowledge. Back in 1990, what was the state recognised by the International Community?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In 1990, the first multi-party elections were conducted, and the process of the independence of the republic started. And in 1990, the Republic of Yugoslavia, the Federal Republic -- the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia was still in operation.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So we're talking about the Federal Republic of Yugoslavia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, and within that state the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Was the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] -- was the Republic of Croatia. Okay, good, let's move on.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, what was the ethnic composition of the area before the outbreak of the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: In the area of the former Municipality of Podravska Slatina, until that time, until 1989 and 1990, relations were tolerable, one could say, but they were encumbered by the supremacy and hegemony of the Serbian minority in all important positions, in the economic sphere, in the political life, in defence, in the police, in the army, in the administration, there were Serbs, and this created a feeling of inferiority among the Croats.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Could you please describe us the situation and the events which led to the conflict?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: In this atmosphere which obtained when relations were already tense, on the 31st of May -- between the 31st of May and the 1st of June, 1990, on a number of buildings, on the facades, that is, in Slatina, in the villages of Sladojevci, Bakric, Bistrica, and Spanat, the nearby villages around Slatina, there were graffiti and slogans written: "This is Greater Serbia, all is Serbia. We shall kill Tudjman." Then there was this iconography with the four letters "S" and other provocative symbols, which provoke the Croatian population and burdened even more inter-ethnic relations, creating a feeling of insecurity with all these slogans and provocations that were -- we could really say were the introduction to the events that followed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Does the name "Dr. Rajskovic" say anything to you?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I am aware of that name. He was the leader of the Serbian Democratic Party, its founder and the main speaker at the founding of the Serbian Democratic Party in the town of Slatina, which was on the 9th of June, 1990, in the afternoon.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you remember what Dr. Rajskovic said according to the mention of the former independent -- future independent Croatian state, how it should be?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, at this gathering, I was guarding the gathering, securing the gathering with some 15 policemen, and I listened to the speech by Dr. Rajskovic and the other leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party who attended the gathering. There were some 5.000 people attending the meeting who had been invited from the nearby villages and surroundings, and the main speaker was Dr. Rajskovic. He spoke in a quite emotionally-charged tone to the masses that had assembled about the need to organise within the Serbian Democratic Party, and he told them, "Brothers, Serbs, if you mean to create a Krajina, do, because in the Ustasha Croatia, there is no room for you, there are no prospects for you," and Slatina was supposed to come the center of an uprising in Slavonia, the Slavonia Knin.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Witness. My specific question was: Do you remember what dimension according to Dr. Rajskovic the Croatian state should have?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, I do. Among the members of the Serbian Democratic Party and in the public, the messages of Dr. Rajskovic were being spread to the effect that Croatia -- that one would be able to see Croatia from the top of the cathedral in Zagreb and that one will be able to tour it in a single day on a bicycle.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: How were the municipal governments working at that time? Did they function?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, immediately after this rally which was held in Slatina, the operation of the executive council was blocked, as was that of the Assembly, which was a multi-party assembly; namely, the Serbian representatives to that assembly no longer wished to attend sessions. And the executive council, which had six Serbs and seven Croats, was a rump council, because the six Serbs, who were representatives to the executive council, did not come to its sessions.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can you describe to us how the Serb population behaved in respect to the Croat population after this event?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, after this event, branches of the Serbian Democratic Party were set up in the field. This fueled tensions, and mistrust was further spread among the multi-ethnic community. The Serbian population looked with mistrust upon the institutions of the Croatian state, those of the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: And how did the Croat population behave or react?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They were in fear, in view of the provocations that I've already referred to, in view of the messages that were being sent, and in view of the overall experiences. Tensions escalated from day to day, I should say, and the atmosphere was quite tense towards the end of 1990.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You already mentioned it, but can you please describe us again what happened on the 9th of June, 1990?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: On the 9th of June, 1990, the Serbian Democratic Party was founded in Slatina, and after that, in September, October and November, organised by the Serbian Democratic Party, there were held the so-called statements of opinions or referenda, which were actually in contravention of the Croatian laws, the laws of the Croatian state and its constitution. The Serbian Democratic Party actually conducted a poll and a referendum. The first referendum asked the question whether the Serbs in Croatia wanted autonomy, and the second was more radical, in terms of its question and demand. The question was whether they wanted an autonomous -- an independent autonomy, their Krajina. And the third referendum, which was conducted with activists of the Serbian Democratic Party going to the houses of the local Serbs, actually sought to achieve the secession of the Republic of Krajina from the Republic of Croatia and its annexation to Serbia and Montenegro, namely, the creation of a greater Serbia.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did Dr. Rajskovic in his speech mention something about the future of the Serb people in Croatia?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, he did say -- he actually ended his speech with this, "Brother Serbs, there can be no happiness and prospects for you here in the Ustasha Croatia. If you want to create a Krajina and a Greater Serbia, do."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You already mentioned the three referenda. Can you tell us if the Croats participated in these referenda?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The Croats did not participate in these referenda, but the referenda were illegal. They had no foundation in the law or regulations. But, nonetheless, the Croatian authorities did not prevent them, precisely with a view not to have the relations between the local population complicated and tensions escalating.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] One question. Had there already been a constitutional amendment at the level of the Croatian Republic, a change in the constitution?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Assembly of the Republic of Croatia had already launched a number of initiatives, and some regulations had been adopted for the achieving of the independence of the Republic of Croatia, but this was being done gradually and in accordance with the requirements of the International Community, which meant a postponement of the disassociation of the former Yugoslavia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you. What I would like to know is the dates. Please recall to us the dates. The 9th of June, the events that you're referring to, on the 9th of June had there already been a change in the Croatian constitution regarding the status of the Serbian ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, they had the same status as the Croatian people, no special status. Everybody was equal under the constitution and law.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to the Yugoslav constitution, based on the socialist -- the Federative Socialist Party of Yugoslavia, that I think that is the name, according to that constitution what was the status of the Serbian people?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] They had the same status as the Croatian people, without anything specific. They were a constituent people, yes. The Croatian people were in the majority. The Serbs and everybody else, the non-Serbs, had equal constitutional and legal rights.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry, I want to come back to the historical background here. When did this change in the status of the Serbian people as a minority take place in the constitution of Croatia?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The constitution of the Republic of Croatia, while Croatia was part of the former Yugoslavia, regulated this issue the way it did. Once Croatia became an independent state, the constitution and the legal legislation adopted by the Assembly regulated the rights of the Croatian people and of all the other minority peoples who lived in the Republic of Croatia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for your answers. I apologise. I need some dates, not in reference to the issue of independence, because as you're well aware of, there were problems because the parliamentary assembly proclaimed independence, and as you said yourself, there were issues which arose at the level of the International Community. Therefore, there were delays in the effective independence. So, please, I beg you, give us a date, a single date on which a change was operated on the status of Serbian people in Croatia and their status was changed into a minority people or something to that effect, if I'm not mistaken. You're bound to remember the date.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I cannot give you the exact date now, because there were a number of decisions and a number of dates; I mean, decisions of the Assembly, the constitutional amendments, the disassociation from the rest of the state. I didn't -- cannot give you the exact dates of all the constitutional changes that took place then. I can give you the details from my concrete line of duty.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, in the police station where you were working, did you have Serbian colleagues or friends with you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In the police station where I was working, there was a mixed ethnic composition. 85 per cent of them were Serbs and 15 per cent of them Croats; until 1990, that is.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good. So you're saying at the police station, 85 per cent were Serbs and 15 per cent Croats. When your Serbian colleagues found out that constitutionally they were a people -- a minority people, what was their reaction?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, they reacted by starting to -- by disobedience to this Croatian state. They returned their weaponry that they had been issued with and their badges, and this is a decision which they brought at the beginning of the changes that I'm talking about. But those who left later, they left with their equipment and with their armaments. Some of them took sick leaves, and they sought in other ways as well not to be in the service of the actual police station that they were working for, the service that they were working for.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Okay. So you've described the atmosphere which existed at the police station. Some of your colleagues decided to leave, to disobey, to no longer wear their uniforms, et cetera. But if that constitutional change had not occurred, do you think they would have behaved in the same way, your Serbian colleagues?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I don't know what their position would have been, whether it would have been like that. But as I've already said, they dominated in the police, in the state administration, in the army and in the economy, and that created a feeling of insecurity among the Croatian people. And probably one of the reasons or the principal reason was the fact that they saw that Croatia was well on the path to independence, and at the invitation, as I've already said, of the leadership of the Serbian Democratic Party, and given the developments which occurred thereafter, they took decisions of this kind. They no longer would be obedient to the Croatian state and their services.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You're referring to the example of the police station that the Serbian dominated, they were 85 per cent, they were a majority. But before 1990, 1989 and 1988, when people went to work for the police, were they entering the police force because they were either Croatian or Serbian or were they entering the police force because they were qualified to become police officers?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The employment policy in the police was conducted at the level of the Ministry of the Interior, which at that time was called "The Republican Secretariat for the Interior" or "for Internal Affairs." The policy at the level of that Republican Secretariat -- or, rather, the party that gave the say so and the blessing for that was such, and it was not only that the Serbs were dominant in the police station in Slatina, even though the population was a majority -- the population -- the Croats were the majority of the population, but this was the situation in all other police stations in this area.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you say "the party," is it the Communist Party?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's correct.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] But you were Croatian. Nobody prevented you from becoming a police officer in Slatina?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, nobody prevented me. There were Croats there, too, but their percentage was the one that I already mentioned.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And was Tito Croatian or Serb?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] He was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand you correctly, in the former Yugoslavia, with the domineering political party, which is the Communist Party, Croatians also had executive responsibilities? Let me repeat my question. In the former Yugoslavia, were Croatians able to reach duties where they had responsibilities or was that limited to Serbian?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] These duties were also performed by Croats, but their representation was unequal compared to that of Serbs, given the overall ethnic mix of the community and of the area from where I also hail and given the overall ethnic composition of the Republic of Croatia. I was talking about an inequality policy of employment when it came to key positions having to do with the functioning of the state, the state apparatus, state services; decision-making positions, in a nutshell.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] When you entered the police force, you must have filled in a form or a file. I assume you probably had to tick either "Croatian" or "Serb" or "Muslim." Was it necessary to indicate your ethnic group?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. In this application for employment with the police, inter alia, with the particulars, one had to state one's ethnicity, and I normally would put that I was a Croat.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Good.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, could you let us know when it happened, this exodus of Serb police officers from the police service? Is it possible to give a date?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I believe that the key development was the 2nd of October, 1990, when there was an attack on the police station in Slatina. On that day, I worked until 6.00 p.m. Then I went home, and a citizen informed me that in the city, in Slatina, there was a concentration of a large group of people that he didn't know, and he assumed there would follow an attack on the police station. I immediately returned to the police station. I informed 15 of my fellow policemen, colleagues, to come to the police station and organise a defence. En route, I could see that crowds were building up and that there was a large group of them heading towards the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Who were these attackers?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The attackers, around 1.000 of them, were Serbs from the general area of Slatina and from the villages in the vicinity who had assembled and come up outside the police station, which is just by the Podravina main highway, which is a very busy route, and so they blocked traffic there. A large number of them were under the influence of alcohol. They were creating a very painful atmosphere, shouting out slogans, "We will not give up our police. This is our police. Let us go to the police. We won't give up or give Yugoslavia." All this actually threatened with the masses breaking into the police station, and their aim was actually to break into the police station and seize some 150 weapons which had been there for the reserve police force, which was there according to establishment. Actually, those weapons belonged to them.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if these attackers have been armed?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. Witness, you took an oath to say the truth, so when I listen to you, I hear that a thousand people came about and there was quite a heavy atmosphere, a lot of tension, and these people were frantic or excited, you're saying that they were shouting, "This is our police," and when I was listening to you I wondered whether you or your friends, your Croatian friends, had put a Croatian flag on the police station, which would have triggered that response.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, no, we didn't hang a flag. The mass of people came organised by the Serbian Democratic Party, led by Milun Karadzic, the president. He was -- then there was Ilija Sasic, Momcilo Subotic, and the leaders of the Serbian Democratic Party, who came to the police station, in front of it, and I provided security for the entrance, the side entrances. And they wanted to speak to Kresimir Libl, the chief of police. I allowed them to do that, and already around 1930 hours or one or two minutes later, at around 8.00 p.m., they were in the police station, discussing matters, and the first events happened at 7.00 p.m.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. Mr. President, the interpreter said that this mass of Serbs who had collected in front of the police station, they referred to the word "Rulja," they used the word "rulja," and I see in the English that you did not use that word, "mob." Now, I demand that the term you used -- that the interpreter using the term "rulja" here to be sent away. He said that a thousand people collected in front of the police station, and he spoke about the atmosphere. The witness did not use the word "rulja," you did not use the word "rulja," in English "mob," so please would you have this interpreter removed from the booth immediately.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Witness, what does the word "rulja" mean in your language, because I didn't talk about any bandits? What does this word "rulja" mean in your language?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In Croatian, the word "rulja" means a mob toppling -- or, rather, unruly mass, an unruly mob, causing a lot of disturbance and so on.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, "rulja" is the worst group of football hooligans that you find at football matches. That would be an adequate -- that would be the kind of translation. Now, there is no more derogatory term for a mass of people in Serbian in the Serbian language than the word "rulja," and it is the same -- Croats use this same word, "rulja," to denote such a mass of hooligans, mob, or so on.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] [Previous translation continues] ... people who came, they were shouting slogans like, "Our police," and things like that. As far as you could see, were these people behaving like hooligans, like an excited bunch of people, or did you say that they were not wearing any weapons, and apart from doing that, they were just shouting slogans? But did they throw stones against the windows of the police station, did they spit? Did it get out of hand in any way? How did they behave?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Now, you see, we're getting to the situation precisely, the situation that was very tense and in which Mato Mesaros, assistant, turned up with another crowd of people on this main road, and he was driving his wife, who was very ill, to the local health centre for medical assistance. Now, on the road -- the people on the road who was present there didn't allow him to go through. They prevented him, they banged on the car, and he found it very difficult to break through this mass of people who had gathered there, and he went to the health centre. Now, after a short space of time where he left his wife, he was coming back with another citizen the same way, he took the same route, and then his car was overturned, completely demolished, and Mato Mesaros was stabbed with knives and screwdrivers and other implements. He was stomach was cut open. He fell on the road -- onto the road, and I and two other policemen -- I was there personally. I intervened, and I took him to a nearby cafe. However, the most extreme person from that mass of people gathered there started to follow us. They demolished the catering establishment, this cafe, smashed the windows and doors. They did not allow the emergency services, first aid, to come to this catering establishment to provide medical assistance. But I had to exit through the garden and the back door and organise the injured person to be taken to hospital in Virovitica, and the car was completely destroyed. Later on, the majority of those who had gathered there, who had weapons, and they attended this meeting which went on until 2200 hours, and they shot hundreds of bullets, they fired hundreds of bullets. And when the mass of people dispersed, you could see all this disarray on the streets.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Very well. Please proceed, Mr. Mussemeyer.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: How did the police officers try to protect their police station?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: We were very resolute in providing security for the police station and to prevent the people who had gathered to enter into the premises, because there'd already been an attack on the police station in Pakrac, Obravac, Bankovac, in the Banovina area, and wherever those attacks took place the rules of the Croatian state were no longer able to be enforced. Anarchy reigned, and we succeeded in providing protection and security and repelling this attack. And truth to tell, we did not use any firearms in doing so or resort to physical force or any other means of coercion and force, except the fact did we took care of the person who was injured and prevented any further massacres that threatened to develop. And so we managed to defend the police station successfully.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have also the Serb police officers participated in this defence?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, a number of Serbs who happened to be policemen and happened to be there, and two others came to help out. They showed their loyalty, displayed loyalty, together with the Croats, and took part in the defence of the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Some minutes ago, you told us that this event was the reason for many Serb police officers to leave the police forces. Did they take their weapons with them?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Most of the Serbs who were in the police force, after this event, when they left, did take their weapons with them. And I've already said that a portion of them did very properly hand over their weapons and all their other equipment when they declared their disobedience, but many others took them with them, and so the ranks of the Croatian police force were very reduced in numbers and equipment. They no longer had the necessary manpower to perform all the police duties that the station ought to perform.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know where these police officers went to? Did they follow certain units?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, that was the end of 1990 and the beginning of 1991, when they left, and most of them later on joined the rebels, the rebel Serb units in the area of Papuk and further afield as well, where they took part in the different units, special platoons, companies, and units that were set up there.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know how was the reaction of the JNA at that time? Was the JNA neutral?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The JNA was not neutral. From the beginning, it took the side of the Serb population, and the leadership, the leaders and people who were over there, were not very well disposed to the Croatian state and the independence of Croatia, so that the JNA, first of all in April 1991, called upon members of Serb ethnicity, the reservists who in the former Yugoslav People's Army attended reserve officers' schools and training courses, and others who had been capacitated in military fields, were called up to the barracks in Virovitica and Slatina for training, and Nasice too, and after these training courses and training exercises, they were provided with weapons and, as such, were sent to the area of Vocin, Papuk, and other areas which were later under the control and occupation where the rebel units were located. So that was the first role. First of all, they called up the reservists and trained them, and after that they were issued with weapons. All the members of the rebel forces were armed after that.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Did all the Serbs receive weapons in that area or not?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, most of the military-able and those who had been called up for training in the barracks that I mentioned were, and those who were later on -- occupied territory, most of them -- practically all of them were armed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Have there been Serbs who refused to get arms?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: There were Serbs who refused and those who remained in the area that was not occupied, and towards the end of May 1991, there was a convoy of weapons, some 40 trucks, which at the time the police had to escort. This convoy came from the Nasice barracks to the broader area of Vocin, Nasice at a distance of 40 kilometres, and the police escorted this convoy full of weapons until the village of Mikleus on the main road, and then the convoy set off to this mountainous area where units had already been established. And we knew there was this transport of weapons, that weapons were being transported, but we couldn't react much. So that was what happening during those areas, in the beginning of June and until the beginning of June it was distributed to the Serbs and members of the rebel units. And a case was recorded of a Serb, surname Kokic, from Jurici, who on that day when the weapons were distributed refused to take a weapon, but overnight they shot at his house. The second day, he set off to the police station in Slatina to report the crime, to report this incident, and he was killed at Ceralije because he refused to accept the arms that were being distributed. That was one case, and later on there were other cases that were recorded in that same area, based on testimony of witnesses who testified.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Were there JNA barracks also in Slatina?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Yes, opposite the police station, and we saw that it was a permanent -- presented a permanent danger to the police, because from the yard of the barracks, there were barrels pointed at the police station. There were two armoured cars, armoured vehicles, as well, and they had their barrels trained on the police station. And the incident we expected to happen did happen on the 4th of August, 1991, when the JNA first of all was motivated by the rebels and provoked a mortar attack on the police station and the location -- locality around the police station. Without any reason, they opened fire on the police station from the armoured vehicles and other weapons, and they targeted the premises next to the barracks, where the hand-over of duty was taking place, and 50 policemen were involved in this takeover or hand-over of duty. However, this hand-over of duty ceremony took place earlier on, so it's very lucky no policemen were killed, although two policemen were seriously wounded. And that part of the police station was quite damaged and was no longer -- could no longer function properly. It was no longer operational.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: According to your investigations, was this attack intentionally or randomly?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The attack was prepared in advance. I've already said that for a number of weeks, heavy weapons were trained on the police station. The army did not communicate with the police station, and that we expected something like that to happen. All that they were looking for was a pretext. And so when several 60-millimetre-calibre shells were fired, and we established this later on on the basis of -- well, the six rebels from above a hill above Slatina, they fired upon the police station and around the police station. This was just taken as a reason for justifying the attack, but we did not provoke it on our side at all, because there were just three or four policemen in the police station at that time, so they were not provoked. All the others were out in the field somewhere.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Has there been later on an explanation from the JNA, why they attacked the police station?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Three days later, officers -- JNA officers arrived at the police station to see what had happened and to find an alibi for the event, which was in no way provoked by our side. Actually, they came in to see the extent of the attack, and since the aim was -- since they aimed at this office where a hand-over of duty had taken place and where there was the highest concentration of manpower, that it was precisely this office that was targeted and shot at. They wanted to shoot at it when this hand-over of duty was being conducted.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: What influence did this event have on the atmosphere of the different ethnicities in the area?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, the event had a strong impact and reverberated amongst the public, and it was yet another message that war was being prepared and the JNA was on the side of the Serb population and that it was just a question -- a matter of days when other armed conflicts would be unleashed. And the aim was to take control of the police station before now by opening fire to incapacitate it to function further, and of course the overall aim was to destroy manpower at a time when they thought that people would be in the police station.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if so-called paramilitary units have been in the area, and if so, since when?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: The paramilitary units that I spoke about, at that time in the area of Vocin and Papuk, had already been established. There was the so-called 12th Slovenian Assault Brigade, similar to the one in World War II, and then there were companies performed. All that had already been established in the woody area, in the forests, where the majority Serb population lived, and then four months later it was occupied and was no longer within the composition and under the power of the Croatian authorities. So for four months, Croatian institutions did not function over there. But at that time already, those paramilitary units had already been formed over there.

utterances.speaker: THE ACCUSED
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Objection. The Prosecutor not only asked a leading question there, but he openly takes the side of the witness, he is on the witness's side. The witness is -- the witness was a member of one side in the civil war, and he speaks about it very openly. And the witness has his own opinion as to what a -- what paramilitary units were or were not. The Prosecutor does not have the right to take the side of the witness. Paramilitary units existed only on the Croatian side. On the Serb side, there was the Territorial Defence and the JNA, and everything was within their composition. There were no paramilitaries, paramilitary units. The Prosecutor must not be allowed to be biased and take the side of anybody in the civil war or in the case of a witness. He must be unbiased in questioning and examining the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, now, the problem related to the paramilitary units. We see what happened. These hundred people come and demonstrate in front of the police station, the Serbian police officers take up arms. And then from a hill, someone shoots at the police station. The three JNA officers then come to conduct an inquiry, quote/unquote. And the Prosecutor is asking you whether this has had an impact on the atmosphere there, and you said, yes, it did. From then on, the Prosecution addresses the issue of paramilitary units. The position of the accused is to say that there are no Serbian paramilitary units, but that there were paramilitary units on the Croatian side. So when these events occurred, as far as you know, were there any paramilitary units, any Serbian paramilitary units, and if so, which ones?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Mr. President, at that time the Croatian police force was the sole armed force which the Croatian state had. In Slatina, there was not a single member of the Croatian Army or Croatian Guards. Now, on the 4th of August, when this event took place, in 1991, the attack on the police station launched by the JNA, it still existed in Slatina right up until the 16th of September, when the Croatian Army took control of the barracks and when all the members of the JNA were released, those who were in the barracks. Now, these paramilitary units, which had been formed and which were referred to by the Prosecutor, really did exist. They were not within any Territorial Defence organisation. They were exclusively made up of ethnic Serbs, and they were formed by people who were preparing an armed uprising. The JNA armed them. And I think that the answer to the question is that it was indeed paramilitaries, paramilitary units, that we were talking about, because the JNA denied having anything to do with them, although in fact it had armed them, and it claimed that they weren't under their command.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] This makes everything more confusing, because on the one hand you say that these paramilitary units were formed by the police, trained by the policemen, and then you add that it was the JNA who provided the weapons. Assuming that what you're saying is true, yes, please clarify this.

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, yes, let me just clarify something. I didn't cause a misunderstanding -- or I might have done. I spoke about earlier on, when members of the police left the police station. They joined up with the paramilitaries later on. So this act of them leaving took place two or three months before. The policemen left the ranks of the police station, and then when these units began to be established, beginning in April of 1991, the paramilitaries, whereas the policemen started leaving in the autumn of 1990. So those policemen who left, they did not form them, but they were members of those units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So you're saying that the Serbian policemen who left the police force joined these paramilitary units?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That's right. That's where they finished up, in those paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Right. So where were these paramilitary units located, and who were they headed by?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The paramilitary units were located in the area of Vocin, for example, and Lager Sekulinci, Zvecevo, stretching towards Pakrac, which is no longer our area but Western Slavonia, and the area that which was not under the control of the Croatian authorities stretched from the Orahovica Municipality, part of the Casinci Municipality, Slatina, right up until Levanoci [phoen] and parts of the Suho Polje Municipality bordering on the area of Western Slavonia in the direction of Pakrac. So those units were in a broader area surrounding Vocin, in the woody areas, and at Lager Sekulinci, which was a military training post when the army was there, training grounds when the army was part of Yugoslav, it was a training grounds previously, but it was given over to the paramilitaries, the paramilitary units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So they were in Sekulinci, where they regrouped. So I put the question to you: Who was their leader? Do you know who their leaders were or didn't you?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I do know. Boro Lukic was their leader. He was a captain. He had previously been educated as a member of the reserve force of the former JNA. And there were others, too, others who had completed reserve officers' school, such as Borivoje Radosaljevic [phoen], I said Lukic, Borivoje as well. Then later on from Novi Sad, Colonel Trbojevic arrived the end of October, and there were also members of the JNA, both reserve officers and active duty officers, who assisted in the establishment of these units and who headed those units as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm sorry.

utterances.speaker: THE INTERPRETER
utterances.text: Microphone, please. Microphone, Your Honour, please.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I need you to shed some light on something, please. You were saying that the JNA was half Serb, so those Serbians that left the police force, why did they join the paramilitaries rather than the JNA? Do you know why the Serbs formed paramilitary groups instead of enrolling in the JNA?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, in Slatina there was a smaller JNA barracks, and they, as policemen, could not have end up in JNA ranks. Rather, they waited up for the setting up of these paramilitary units which started to be formed in the beginning of April 1991, and most of them ended up there, as evidenced by records. The complete organisation, their numbers, the number of issued weapons, all this is reflected in the documentation left by the paramilitary units when they withdrew from the area. So these lists contain every single man who was a part of these units, and it is on the basis of such data that we actually saw where they ended up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] And could they join on a volunteer basis in the JNA or not?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] According to my information, none of them, on leaving the Croatian police, ended up as a volunteer within the JNA, and almost all of them ended up as members of these insurgent units.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] You said that there was a log, and by looking at the log it was possible to determine where they joined. What's the log you're talking about, where is it coming from?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Well, this was a list of the units, the platoons, the companies, the battalions, indicating the names, surname, year of birth, the number of the issued weapons, the date of arrival to the unit, so it was a complete documentation, and this is in the possession of the Croatian prosecutor's office and it certainly does show who played what role during those developments which took place in the area of our municipality.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] How do you know that the Croatian prosecutor has a list of all the people who were members of paramilitary units? How do you know about that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I know that because I was the one who coordinated the activities of some 20 crime inspectors who were gathering data on all the developments during and after the war. After the area had been abandoned by paramilitary formations. The documentation which was found in the command of the insurgent units at Zvecevo remained there and all of it was handed over to the Croatian police, actually to the Croatian police station in which I worked, and I personally saw and actually compiled and completed all these lists. Having completed the files, we submitted all the files to the prosecution organs, and I believe that the originals are still in the police stations. So they were found in-situ in the command, and they were submitted to the prosecution and to judicial bodies as well.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand correctly, after the war you coordinated activities overseeing a team of inspectors in charge of investigating the crimes that had occurred, and within the framework of your investigation you came up with a list of all the people enrolled or enlisted in the paramilitary units, and this list was handed over to the Croatian prosecutor in charge of the investigation; is that it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] That is correct. That was an integral part of the crime investigation and of all the files, normally with witness statements, statements by victims, so this is just a part of the mosaic which was composed in order to shed light on all the events that transpired while this area was under occupation and on the individual roles of the individual persons during the war events.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The Prosecution, this document, this list the witness is talking about, have you had it and have you communicated it to Mr. Seselj?

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: They are on the exhibit list, and as far as I know they have been disclosed to Mr. Seselj. I will use parts of it in the -- when I continue with the witness.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It's now a quarter past 4.00. We're going to take a break for 20 minutes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] We now resume the hearing. The floor is to the Prosecution.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, before we finished we spoke about paramilitary units. Do you know if they erected barricades in your region, and if so, since when?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: They erected barricades whereby they blocked the area which was later occupied, the area where the Croatian state did not function. The barricades were set up sometime around mid-August, from the 14th of August, 1991. On the 18th of August, namely, four days after the takeover of the police station in Vocin. And in that same year, on the 14th of August, the waiter Ilic was taken away from a hotel in Vocin by paramilitary units. So these events in mid-August coincided, and from that time on the Croatian state was no longer functional in the area. There was no communication along the roads because barricades of felled trees had been set up and also manned by guards along the roads.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Thank you, Mr. Matovina. Before we come to the events in Vocin, I first wanted to come to the events in Cetekovac. Can you describe us what happened there on the beginning of September 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: More precisely, on the 4th of September, 1991, around 9.00, paramilitary units from the Vocin area, or more precisely from the Lager Sekulinci locality, in an organised and coordinated attack, attacked the village of Cetekovac, Cojlug and Balinci, that is to say, three villages predominantly populated by Croats. This special platoon, some 60 men strong, this paramilitary formation headed by Boro Lukic, raided the village and killed 22 civilians and two policemen, who happened to be in the village because they are from that village and have houses in the village. Simultaneously as the attack was taking place on these villages, Boro Lukic's unit, with about 130 men, actually posted flank guards -- flank guards on the villages so that Croatian forces were unable to assist the villagers, and some people who actually were returning to the village were ambushed and killed. As I said, 22 civilians and 2 policemen were killed in the village. Two bodies were burned. The village was looted. Almost half of the houses in the village of Cetekovac were torched, were burnt down.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, since you're a witness of fact, could you please tell us whether you are telling about events you were a witness to directly or are you telling us about things you've heard of by hearsay?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] I'm describing this event on the basis of the crime investigation that I conducted, also on the basis of the documents that were obtained, and on the basis of witness statements, as well as on the basis of an on-site investigation which was done on the second or third day, as soon as it was possible, given the fire that was constantly opened at that position. So after the complete -- the investigation was complete and the coordination effort which I was in charge of, as well as after the complaint, the criminal complaint against the perpetrators had been written and filed.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Thank you for shedding that light. A small detail. You drafted the criminal report, so the complaint given to the prosecution was drafted by you, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes, I personally wrote the criminal report, criminal complaint.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] In your report, who is responsible for the events?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Heading that unit was Reserve Captain Borivoje Lukic, and the other members were identified in talks, most of them, that is, and they were people from the nearby villages, from the neighbouring villages. The surviving witnesses were astonished. They couldn't believe that the massacre had been perpetrated by their acquaintances, by their neighbours, who had put on JNA uniforms that the JNA had distributed to them, along with the weapons, and that they had committed that massacre. So most of them were from the nearby adjacent neighbouring villages; acquaintances and friends, in fact.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know the reasons why they attacked this village?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, first of all, they erected the barricades and prevented traffic from moving along the road between the attacked villages and this part that was later occupied. There was practically no reason whatsoever for that. I believe that the sole reason was hate, because these people -- some of these people who actually did not expect that attack were either in the catering establishment, in the street, in their yards. It was a sudden and wholly unexpected attack.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if Boro Lukic had a nickname?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: What we learned later is that his nickname was "Munja."

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if he was an SDS member?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, he probably was. He was an electrician by trade. He worked in an enterprise called "Gaj." He had completed a school for reserve officers and had a reserve rank of -- the rank of reserve captain prior to these conflict erupting, and he was the first to go to Lager Sekulinci, where members of the paramilitary unit were being trained.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know what his approach towards Croats was?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: He was -- he held extremist and radical views, obviously, given that all this that I have described -- that he was an actor in all these that I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Where did you know this from? Did you know him from before?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: I did know him personally, because I, too, used to work in Gaj Enterprise. All the time up to the beginning of these events, he was there, in that enterprise, working there. But as I said, he was among the first to organise this military formation.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know if the attackers on this village have been assisted by someone?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, according to the documentation that we found at the seat -- at the command of the insurgent units, the attack on the village of Cetekovac had been militarily planned, so we found a map with specific activities of the units indicated, the directions of activities, the raiding of the village much Cetekovac, Cojlug and Balinci, the flank guards to be posted. And according to what we saw, it is obvious that militarily-capable men, persons, had drawn up that plan. The plan was made by a person who was acquainted with military tactics and strategy, and it was actually according to that plan that the attack was indeed carried out on these villages. This could have only been drawn up by a person who had completed JNA schools or a person who was a reserve officer of the JNA.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: You already told us about Lager Sekulinci. Can you tell us what this Lager was about again?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: This is a military training ground amid a forest which has the necessary logistics for the training of military units, the necessary buildings, proofing ground, training ground, otherwise used by the JNA. And then later it was as given by the JNA to the Territorial Defence, which then ceded that ground to the insurgent units, where they also had a part of their command.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Do you know what happened at Lager Sekulinci?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: Well, at Lager Sekulinci, apart from that being the locality where the command and a part of the units were located, people who were abducted would also be taken there and maltreated and beaten up. A number were also killed. For instance, Franjo Banovac, who was taken away from Hum, he was tortured and killed at Lager Sekulinci and his body was found in the woods two months after the units had left. Also, the waiter Ilic had been taken to Lager Sekulinci and executed there. Later, parts of his body were found. And all those who had been apprehended or taken there were maltreated and tortured, so that was a place where those Croats who were -- Croats who had been either liquidated or released were held in captivity there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, regarding what happened in Lager Sekulinci, did you carry out an investigation so as to be able to understand what happened? What sources is your evidence based on? Prosecution, could you, at the beginning of a new area, try to clarify these matters, basically on the basis of what is the evidence relying on. So for Sekulinci, did you carry out an investigation?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Yes. This was a component part of the investigation that we undertook throughout the area. We found the bodies of Sid -- of Franjo Banovac, and we had an on-site investigation also conducted, and parts of the body of the waiter Ilic also. There was another policeman, Velickovic, and then there was Kreso Doric who was tortured. His body exists, as does documentation to that effect. There are also the statements of a number of witnesses who were up there, as well as written documentation, which is an integral part of this entire investigation that I have described.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: At this moment --

utterances.speaker: JUDGE LATTANZI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Sorry. The conclusions of the investigation, were they confirmed by any order, decision?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] All that was submitted to the state prosecutor's office, and it is -- the processing of all these case files is still underway. I left the police some eight years ago, so these investigations are still ongoing. Other people are conducting them. It is still in the ongoing stage. Some investigations are still going on, whereas some cases have been completed.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Madam Registrar, at this moment I would like to have 65 ter number -- the document of 65 ter number 451 on the monitor, if it's possible.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Witness, could you look at this document and let us know what it is about?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: This is from the health centre. This is a medical document for Darko Bozickovic, who was abducted by Zoran Miscevic and other paramilitary unit members and taken to Lager Sekulinci, where he sustained bodily injury, after which he asked for medical assistance.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Can I have this document moved into evidence?

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Registrar.

utterances.speaker: THE REGISTRAR
utterances.text: Your Honours, that will be Exhibit P429.

utterances.speaker: MR. MUSSEMEYER
utterances.text: Mr. Matovina, could you please let us know what happened at the police station in Vocin in August of 1991?

utterances.speaker: DJURO MATOVINA
utterances.text: More precisely, on the 18th of August, 1991, Borivoje Lukic, with his special unit, platoon of specials, took the military -- the police station in Vocin, took off the flag of the Republic of Croatia off it, and burnt it there. They hoisted the flag of the Republic of Serbia in its place, and at that point officially all the policemen actually aligned themselves and started to be in the service of the insurgency authorities that had been established. Up until that time, they had not been in the service -- they had not been loyal to the state of Croatia either, but at that point they did this officially. On that occasion, all the weapons that happened to be there was seized, as were all the automobiles and all the equipment. Two policemen who sometimes declared themselves as Yugoslavs and at other times as Croats were designated as disloyal, and they were proclaimed unnecessary, redundant, and could no longer serve in the police station that had been taken.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Witness, please, what you're just saying actually is along the lines of what I was saying at the beginning of the afternoon. You're saying that on the 18th of August, 1991, Lukic had taken the flag of the Croatian Republic and burnt it. In August 1991, the Republic of Croatia had not been yet recognised as a state. Do you agree with that?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It had its flags and symbols and constitution. Well, on the building, it was the flag of the Republic of Croatia that was hoisted up.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] Let's backtrack a bit. Before Tito's disappearance, in the Federative Republic of Yugoslavia, in Croatia, was there a Croatian flag being waved or posted on the walls of a police station or was there one single flag, the Yugoslavian flag, or were there two flags?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] It was like this: Before, the flag that was hoisted was both that of the Republic of Croatia and Yugoslavia. But on the flag of the Republic of Croatia, you had the socialist symbols, such as -- or, rather, like in the Republic of Yugoslavia, whereas on this other flag that was raised at the police station, you had the symbols and the flag of the Republic of Croatia; that is to say, the new flag was raised there.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] So if I understand correctly, this flag that had been put on the police station was put there in anticipation, because Croatia at the time was not really a state, so the flag that was there was the future flag of Croatia, wasn't it?

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] No, it was already a state, but the procedure of settling everything was still in process. Croatia already had its constitution and its flag, and that flag, which was in conformity with the constitution, was the one that was put up on the police station. That was the flag that was taken down and set fire to and replaced by the flag of the Republic of Serbia.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The flag which was burnt, is it similar to the one which is in the --

utterances.speaker: THE WITNESS
utterances.text: [Interpretation] The same flag, yes.

utterances.speaker: JUDGE ANTONETTI
